about.title: Crescent City Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Crescent City is a small coastal community, but defective products cause the same kinds of harm here as anywhere else — whether it's a malfunctioning vehicle part on Rt 101, a faulty tool used at a local job, or an appliance that fails at home. California law generally applies strict liability to these cases, meaning an injured person doesn't have to prove the manufacturer was careless — only that the product itself was defective and that the defect caused harm. This matters in a town like Crescent City, where residents may not have easy access to specialized product liability counsel nearby. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself; we simply connect people who've been hurt by defective products with an independent attorney in California who can evaluate the situation. If a product failed you — in design, in manufacturing, or in the warnings that came with it — it's worth having someone look at the facts before you decide anything else. There's no cost to get connected, and no obligation to move forward.

whyChoose.title: What to Know About Product Liability Law in California

items.title: Strict Liability Can Simplify Your Case
items.desc: Under California law, you generally don't need to prove the manufacturer was negligent — just that the product was defective and caused your injury. This can make the path to a claim more direct than other injury cases.

items.title: Multiple Parties May Share Responsibility
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers can all potentially be held liable for a defective product. An attorney can help identify who was actually responsible for the defect that caused harm.

items.title: Keeping the Product Matters
items.desc: Because these cases often hinge on showing a design, manufacturing, or warning defect, preserving the actual product involved is important evidence. An attorney can advise on how to protect that evidence early on.

items.question: What counts as a product defect under California law?
items.answer: California recognizes three main types: design defects, manufacturing defects, and failure-to-warn defects. A design defect means the product was inherently unsafe even when made correctly; a manufacturing defect means something went wrong during production; a failure-to-warn defect means the product lacked adequate instructions or warnings about known risks.

items.question: Do I need to prove the manufacturer was careless?
items.answer: No — California generally applies strict liability to product defect cases, so the focus is on whether the product itself was defective and caused your injury, not on proving carelessness. This is different from many other injury claims that hinge on showing negligence.

items.question: I live near 5th Street or US-101 in Crescent City — does that matter for a product claim?
items.answer: Where the injury happened doesn't change the underlying law, but local details like which roads or areas are involved can matter for gathering evidence and understanding what happened. An independent attorney familiar with Del Norte County can help sort through those specifics.

items.question: What should I do with the product that caused my injury?
items.answer: Try to keep it exactly as it was at the time of the incident, including any packaging, instructions, or parts, since this evidence is often central to a product liability claim. Avoid repairing or discarding it until you've spoken with an attorney about preserving it properly.
